Photograph: Yui Mok/PA View image in fullscreen In 2024, M&S reported a third of underwear sales were made by people under 30. Photograph: Yui Mok/PA Marks & Spencer Knickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless panties isn’t as outrageous as it seems Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say Lauren Cochrane Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he news that Marks & Spencer is selling Ann Summers crotchless knickers on their website has been greeted – as might be expected – with outrage online, being described as everything from “tawdry” to “S & M” . But it could be this is just the latest evolution in what the UK’s biggest underwear retailer has available for the smalls drawer. In recent years, the store has sold vastly different options through its own products, ranging from full-brief knickers to thongs, period knickers and those that can be used by women who wear stomas . The introduction of other brands in clothing came five years ago, with underwear included. Ann Summers – which is selling bras and chemises as well as knickers on the M&S website – lines up alongside lingerie brands including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein. Catherine Shuttleworth, the chief executive of retail consultancy Savvy, sees it as part of wider strategy. “They’ve started introducing brands to bring them into sectors that probably isn’t their core,” she says. “And this is another one. It’s just a little bit more eye-catching.” View image in fullscreen The offending crotchless thong being sold by M&S, which has been called ‘tawdry’ Photograph: M&S Shuttleworth describes M&S underwear as a “national obsession” and there’s little doubt the store remains a must-visit for anyone restocking their underwear drawer. If its long-term popularity might have meant it was perceived as a bit mumsy for younger people, that has changed recently. In 2024, the store reported that people under 30 made up a third of underwear sales – double that of 2023. View image in fullscreen The Ann Summers knickers are sold on M&S’s website alongside other retailers including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein. Photograph: M&S Shuttleworth says the introduction of Ann Summers could be about continuing to engage this demographic. “They are always innovating for every stage of your life,” she says. “And I think this is a gap in their category. Ann Summers is a byword for sex, isn’t it?” This echoes the message coming from the retailer itself. In a statement, an M&S spokesperson said: “Our ‘brands at M&S’ strategy is all about giving customers greater choice through carefully selected third-party brands that complement our existing M&S offer. Ann Summers is one of the latest brands to join [M&S online], helping broaden our underwear and nightwear offer.” There is also, of course, the publicity factor. “It doesn’t really matter whether they sell any crotchless pants or not, we’re all going to be talking about it,” says Shuttleworth. “You might also go online to look. You might not buy those, but you’ll think: ‘I could do with replacing my pants.’” M&S has sold underwear since the 1920s and fitted bras since 1947 . It was the first retailer to sell pre-shrunk cotton underwear in 1965, and by 1976 knickers were the biggest export – nearly 4m pairs were sold internationally every year. Fashion dictated different styles – from the “hip-hugger” styles in the 60s to thongs, which reached the apex of popularity in the mid- 00s. In 2016, the store sold 60m pairs of knickers a year, with Brazilian knickers replacing the thong. The style, which reveals some of the wearer’s bum, made up 10% of those sales. By 2021, thongs were back , thanks to the popularity of low rise jeans. According to the retailer’s website, the No 1 bestseller now is a five-pack of white full briefs. View image in fullscreen Experts have said that M&S have always followed trends, including lace designs a world away from basics. Photograph: PR Image Lorraine Topper, a researcher at The Underpinnings Museum , argues the reaction around the crotchless knickers is disproportionate – because the store does stock sexier styles along with basics. “M&S have always followed fashion with regard to their lingerie designs,” she says. “For some reason, it’s the multipack of full briefs that sticks in people’s heads when you talk about their underwear, rather than, for example, the beautiful lace designs from the Rosie Exclusively range.” She describes the outrage as “a fuss over nothing … Open-crotch underwear for women was the norm before the 1920s so this type of garment isn’t quite as scandalous as we might first think.” Explore more on these topics Marks & Spencer Retail industry Underwear news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail

https://www.illawarramercury.com.au/stor.text: Hungary's only nuclear power plant will shut down for the first time in its history due to record-low water levels on the Danube River, Prime Minister Peter Magyar says, adding that the plant might not come back online for several weeks as the river is expected to continue receding. The Paks nuclear plant, about 90km south of the capital Budapest, is operating at less than half its normal capacity, producing 965 megawatts of power rather than the usual 2000. The plant uses water from the Danube to cool its reactors, but the exceptionally low water level has tested the ability of pumps to bring sufficient quantities into the plant. Speaking at a news conference at the plant on Friday, Magyar said further reductions in output were imminent later that day, and the entire plant would likely be powered down by Tuesday or Wednesday. He stressed the shutdown could be performed safely and posed no risk to the public or environment. The Soviet-built, four-reactor plant at Paks accounts for nearly half of Hungary's electricity production. If it is powered down, it will be the first time in its 44 years of service. Hungary and much of Central Europe has been in a prolonged drought in recent months, disrupting tourism, agriculture and industry and confronting residents with the realities of climate change. Water levels are not expected to rise on the Danube in the coming days or even weeks as no significant rainfall is forecast. Magyar said the Danube's water level had risen on only three occasions in the month of August in the past 20 years, and added the level at Paks could recede to as low as negative 144cm - far below the previous record of negative 98cm in 2018. A level of negative 134cm required the full powering down of the plant, he said. A negative reading means the river has fallen below the gauge's zero reference level, not that the river is empty. Hungary's government has requested that large companies that consume large quantities of energy voluntarily reduce their consumption to help stabilise the energy supply, particularly in peak demand hours at night. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8vg.text: Figure caption, BBC Verify has confirmed the footage was filmed in western Yemen. By Thomas Copeland Â and Â Charlotte Green ,Â BBC Verify Published 17 September 2026 Footage verified by the BBC shows the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen. The US-made aircraft was "downed using a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile" as it "conducted hostile operations" over the Marib region, according to a Houthi statement on Wednesday. Experts have told BBC Verify the incident is a "propaganda coup" that shows the Houthis' military capability has advanced and they are prepared to further escalate its conflict with Saudi Arabia. Using satellite imagery to match features in the landscape seen in the footage, BBC Verify was able to pinpoint the crash site to an isolated location in the hills west of the Yemeni city of Marib. The long-running conflict between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis has escalated in the last week after the armed group launched an offensive against pro-government forces. This led to the Houthis seizing key territory near the south-west coast, close to vital international shipping channels in the Bab al-Mandab strait. In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number. The fate of of the crew is not known. The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile. BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment. Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran. "They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said. Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains. "An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added. BBC Verify used the position of the sun and satellite imagery to locate the distinctive landscape seen in the footage - including cliff faces and hills - to an isolated mountainous area about 25 miles (40km) west of Marib. Satellite imagery published on Wednesday also shows a new dark shadow at the same location, which appears consistent with scorch or burn marks at a crash site. The aircraft in the wreckage has been independently identified by Nick Brown, a weapons expert from military intelligence company Janes, as an F-15 Strike Eagle. He based his analysis on distinctive elements seen in the footage including the tail fin arrangement, radar antenna and missile warning system sensors. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, A similar Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 Strike Eagle formed part of an escort for US President Donald Trump during a visit to Saudi Arabia last year The four-digit tail number visible on the wreckage also appears to be consistent with that of an F-15 Strike Eagle operated by the 55th Squadron of the Royal Saudi Air Force based at King Khalid Air Base near the city of Khamis Mushait in south-west Saudi Arabia. This base, about 245 miles (392 km) from the crash site, was targeted last week by what the Houthis described as a "barrage of missiles and drones". Satellite imagery analysed by BBC Verify appears to show damage to at least three aircraft hangars or shelters. The base is one of a series of high-profile Saudi targets struck by the Houthis in recent days including an oil refinery in the city of Jizan. Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday it had destroyed a Houthi drone close to the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, which the Houthis have denied targeting. The group said on Thursday that Saudi Arabia had launched 40 air strikes against Yemen over the past 24 hours. Photograph: Tatan Syuflana/AP Indonesia Indonesia wildfire fuelled by El Niño razes almost 300 homes Hundreds of people displaced in Bangka Belitung province as shift in wind direction drove blaze towards settlement Agence France-Presse in Bangka Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.44 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said on Tuesday as the country battles devastating blazes and haze. Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, said the head of South Bangka regency, Riza Herdavid. ‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan population Read more “They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.” The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people had fled the village. “My house is gone,” said Leni, a 55-year-old woman staying at a shelter with her family. “There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything.” Another survivor, Haryanti, 50, said strong winds had fuelled the flames, which had torn through homes that were made mostly of wood. “I immediately ran to save myself. None of my belongings survived ... only the clothes on my back,” she said. Riza said the village had been built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, but which was converted into a housing complex last year. Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region Read more Indonesia regularly has wildfires during the dry season, but they have been more intense this year because of the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is forecast to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago. Experts also point to slash-and-burn land clearances that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo islands. This year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused air pollution spikes in Singapore and Malaysia. Thick smoke in a province of Borneo has also grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency. Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered the government on Monday to mobilise maximum efforts to extinguish wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places. The cabinet secretary, Teddy Indra Wijaya, said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel on the ground.
